CHIEF COMPLAINT
Nonhealing foot ulcer

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient presents with a nonhealing foot ulcer on the right foot that has been present for approximately two months. Patient reports the ulcer recently became red and started draining, which prompted concern about healing. Patient believes the ulcer may have resulted from walking barefoot at Dewey Beach. Patient reports the wound sometimes throbs but denies specific sharp pain. Patient is concerned about the redness and drainage, which are new findings. Patient has diabetes which is believed to be a major contributing factor to poor wound healing. Patient takes diabetes medication but does not regularly check blood sugar levels. Patient reports last A1C was approximately 10. Patient's primary care physician had prescribed antibiotics but patient has not yet picked them up from the pharmacy.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient reports occasional throbbing at the ulcer site without specific sharp pain. Patient denies fever. Patient reports increased pressure sensation with palpation but no distinct pain.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Diabetes

MEDICATIONS
Patient takes medication for diabetes but does not recall specific names. Patient was prescribed antibiotics by primary care physician but has not yet filled the prescription.

ALLERGIES
Not discussed.

FAMILY HISTORY
Not discussed.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient was at Dewey Beach where the foot injury occurred. Patient works as an ambulance driver.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs normal. No fever present. Right foot exam reveals a 1 by 2 inch circular wound on the dorsal aspect of the lateral right foot, just proximal to the fifth metatarsophalangeal joint. Wound shows redness, drainage, and edema around the area. No necrosis noted. No odor appreciated. No bony exposure. Palpation elicits sensation of increased pressure without distinct pain.

RESULTS
X-ray of right foot shows no evidence of osteomyelitis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Diabetic foot ulcer with infection on right foot. Plan includes: (1) Order ankle-brachial index to assess blood supply to the foot; (2) Perform debridement to remove dead tissue; (3) Prescribe clindamycin 400 mg twice daily for 7 days to treat infection; (4) Provide surgical shoe to reduce pressure on foot for the next month; (5) Follow up visit in 2 weeks for reassessment and possible repeat debridement. Patient advised to call office if any issues arise and to seek urgent care or emergency department if fever develops or other emergencies occur.
